# Natenberg Model Assumptions Audit

## What this decides

"The accuracy of values generated by a theoretical pricing model rests on two points: the accuracy of the assumptions upon which the model is based, and the accuracy of the inputs into the model." This skill owns the first point.

Given a specific option position and the market it trades in, it decides:

1. Which of the six assumptions is materially broken in this market, right now.
2. Which direction each break biases the theoretical value (too high, too low, or unreliable in both directions).
3. Whether you may trade off the model's numbers, must haircut them, or must set the sheets aside and decide from experience.

"Traditional pricing model" means what Natenberg's footnote 1 says it means: "those that are most commonly used: the Black-Scholes model and its variations, the Cox-Ross-Rubenstein model, or the Whaley model."

Decide by: if the audit ends with "the model is fine," you have not audited it. Every one of the six is violated in every real market. The question is only which violation is large enough to change the trade.

Boundary: `katz-optimization-without-curvefitting` guards a trading system's parameters against curve-fitting; this audits a pricing model's structural assumptions, which is a different object.

## The six assumptions, and how each one fails

The list, verbatim, book p385:

1. Markets are frictionless
   a. The underlying contract can be freely bought or sold, without restriction
   b. There are no tax consequences associated with trading
   c. Everyone can borrow and lend money freely, and one interest rate applies to all transactions
   d. There are no transaction costs
2. Interest rates are constant over the life of an option
3. Volatility is constant over the life of an option
4. Trading is continuous with no gaps in the price changes of an underlying instrument
5. Volatility is independent of the price of the underlying contract
6. Over short periods of time the percent price changes in an underlying contract are normally distributed, resulting in a lognormal distribution of underlying prices at expiration

### 1. Markets are frictionless

| Sub-assumption | Real world violation | Bias / consequence | What the trader does |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1a, free to buy or sell the underlying (futures) | Exchanges set daily price limits. At the limit, trading halts until the market comes off limit; if it does not, no trading until the next business day. | Consequences "usually not severe," because circumventions exist. | Trade the cash market instead; or trade a futures spread where one leg is not locked (wants June, June is up limit, March still trades: buy the June/March spread, then buy back the March future, leaving net long June); or, if futures are locked but options are not, trade synthetic long/short futures. |
| 1a (stock) | Prohibitions on selling stock not owned, and restrictions on when short sales can be made. | Put prices become inflated compared to call prices; all conversions and reversals appear mispriced with respect to their theoretical values. | Many stock option traders carry some long stock so they are always in a position to sell stock if the need arises. |
| 1a (tender offers) | A live tender offer distorts time spreads (Ch 5) and boxes (Ch 12). | Traders may be forced to exercise calls with time value remaining because no stock can be borrowed to carry a short position; a box may trade above its theoretical value if a partial tender offer is made and early exercise is possible. | Treat time spreads and boxes as un-modelled while a tender is live. |
| 1b, no tax consequences | Occasional tax considerations. | "for most market participants these are usually minor." | "Differences in tax consequences, or changing tax consequences, rarely make one strategy better than another." A trader is unlikely to ask (and "nor should most traders" ask) what the tax consequence of a trade is. Footnote 2 exceptions: portfolio management, and stock option strategies involving dividends where dividends are taxed differently from gains and losses. |
| 1c, borrow and lend freely | "a more serious weakness." Real traders have no unlimited borrowing capacity. A later margin call may force liquidation prior to expiration, yet all models, even those allowing early exercise, assume the trader always has the choice of holding to expiration. | Inability to meet margin, and therefore to maintain the position, makes model values less reliable. | "Experienced traders learn to consider the risk of a position not only from the standpoint of how much the position might lose if things go wrong, but how much margin might be required to maintain the position over the life of the options. A trader should always have sufficient margin money available to meet this latter requirement." |
| 1c, one rate for all transactions | The borrowing rate is not the lending rate. Margin money borrowed at one rate earns a lower rate on deposit at the clearing house. | The spread is a loss the model is unaware of. "the greater the difference between borrowing and lending rates, the less reliable will be the values generated by the model." | Haircut model values by the borrow / lend spread. |
| 1d, no transaction costs | "The most serious flaw in the frictionless markets hypothesis." Brokerage fees, clearing fees, exchange membership. Costs accrue at initiation, at liquidation, and every time an adjustment is made. | A strategy that looks sensible on model values may not be worth doing once costs are counted. Impact is greatest on high-gamma, delta-neutral strategies requiring many adjustments. | Price the whole adjustment path, not just entry and exit. For a high-gamma delta-neutral program, cost is a first-order term that scales with gamma. |

Footnote 3: the possibility of having to post additional *variation* margin (as opposed to margin money) in a futures option market **is** incorporated into most models. "This is why a conversion or reversal in a futures option market may not be delta neutral."

### 2. Interest rates are constant over the life of an option

What the model assumes: the riskless rate over the life of the option, in most markets the government-securities rate for the corresponding term. A US trader selling 3-month straddles is assumed by the model to have invested the credit in 3-month T-bills; holding both to expiration effectively locks in that one rate.

The violation: few traders actually buy government securities. Proceeds go into a trading account at a variable rate. A trader can lend to the government but cannot borrow from it at the same rate, and bank borrowing may itself be variable. Most transactions are therefore subject to a constantly changing rate, not a fixed riskless one.

Bias direction and severity: **small**. "interest rates usually do not change in a way which will have a significant impact on an option's value, at least in the short run." The rate effect is a function of time to expiration, and most listed options run under nine months, so rates would have to change violently to affect anything but the most deeply in-the-money options. Option values are far more sensitive to underlying price and to volatility.

Two exceptions that still need watching:

1. Stock-option time spreads (Ch 8, Figure 8-15), but rates must move several percentage points over a short period to matter.
2. LEAPS and other long-dated equity options, where "the consequences of changing interest rates may well become more of a concern."

**Figure 18-1** (book p389). Stock price = 100; Time to expiration = 2 years; Volatility = 20%; Dividend = 0. Deltas in parentheses.

| | 2% | 4% | 6% | 8% | 10% | 12% | 14% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 80 call | 25.48 (86) | 27.90 (89) | 30.34 (91) | 32.77 (93) | 35.17 (95) | 37.54 (96) | 39.87 (97) |
| 80 put | 2.34 (-14) | 1.75 (-11) | 1.29 (-9) | .94 (-7) | .67 (-5) | .47 (-4) | .33 (-3) |
| 100 call | 13.10 (61) | 15.08 (66) | 17.20 (71) | 19.42 (76) | 21.72 (80) | 24.09 (84) | 26.50 (87) |
| 100 put | 9.17 (-39) | 7.39 (-34) | 5.89 (-29) | 4.63 (-24) | 3.59 (-20) | 2.75 (-16) | 2.08 (-13) |
| 120 call | 5.95 (36) | 7.22 (41) | 9.00 (47) | 10.28 (52) | 12.05 (58) | 13.96 (64) | 16.00 (69) |
| 120 put | 21.24 (-64) | 18.00 (-59) | 15.10 (-53) | 12.54 (-48) | 10.29 (-42) | 8.35 (-36) | 6.70 (-31) |

The read Natenberg pulls out: "Note particularly how quickly the 120 put drops below its parity value of 20.00." It crosses parity between the 4% column (18.00) and the 6% column (15.10).

What the trader does: on anything short-dated, stop worrying about the rate and go audit volatility instead. On LEAPS, re-price across a rate band rather than a point rate. In a high interest rate environment, treat a long-term in-the-money American put as an early-exercise candidate, because everyone will prefer to exercise the put to earn a high rate of interest on the proceeds from the sale of the stock.

### 3. Volatility is constant over the life of the option

What the model assumes: the input volatility sets the magnitude of price changes over the life of the option, and, the hidden second half, "occurrences of each particular magnitude will be evenly distributed over the life of the option." Two-standard-deviation changes evenly distributed among one-SD changes, three-SD evenly among one- and two-SD, and so on.

The violation (Figures 18-2a and 18-2b): two daily bar charts of the same underlying with exactly the same volatility, 16.7%, but opposite ordering. In 18-2a all the large price changes come early in the option's life; in 18-2b all the large price changes come late. The real world bunches: periods of high volatility where two- and three-SD moves cluster, periods of low volatility where one-SD moves cluster. "A graph of historical volatility is never a straight line." The model sees only "16.7%" and cannot tell the two scenarios apart.

The worked case: buy the 105 straddle, correctly assuming 16.7%, delta-hedging over the life. The model says the P&L is identical in either scenario. It is not. The underlying passes through 105 both at the beginning and at the end, so the 105 call and put are at-the-money in both periods, and at-the-money options have the highest gamma. Short-term at-the-money options always have greater gammas than long-term at-the-money options, so volatility occurring in the latter part of the life (18-2b) has a much greater impact than the same volatility early (18-2a). Gamma determines both the magnitude and the frequency of the adjustment process, so movement back and forth through the exercise price late in the life "will require larger and larger adjustments, each of which is favorable to the holder of the 105 straddle." The 18-2a adjustments are relatively small because the movement is less dramatic.

**Bias rule, verbatim (book p393):** "Consequently, even if one knows the actual volatility over the life of an option, a model will tend to **undervalue at-the-money options in a rising volatility market, and overvalue at-the-money options in a falling volatility market**."

Preceding line: "Through experience most traders have come to the conclusion that the order in which volatility occurs does matter. It matters especially for at-the-money options, because they have the greatest gammas."

Structural exception, interest-rate products: some contracts by their nature change volatility characteristics over time. As a bond approaches maturity its price moves inexorably toward par; at maturity it has a fixed and known value regardless of interest rates. "Clearly, one cannot assume that the price of the bond follows a random walk through time." Even assuming rates move randomly with constant rate-volatility, interest-rate instruments change volatility over time because instruments of different maturities have different sensitivities to changes in interest rates. Add the fact that rates vary by maturity and "a traditional Black-Scholes type model is obviously inadequate for the evaluation of such products." Use a special interest-rate model (footnote 5: Ho and Lee 1986; Heath, Jarrow and Morton 1992).

What the trader does: refuse the model's claim that the timing of volatility is irrelevant. Ask where in the option's life you expect the movement, and mark up at-the-money options when you expect volatility to rise, down when you expect it to fall. Do not switch to a stochastic volatility model unless you can specify its extra structure (see below).

### 4. Trading is continuous

Definitions, verbatim:

- Diffusion process: "smooth and continuous changes from one price to the next, with no gaps between consecutive prices. Moreover, the longer the period of time between price readings, the greater the dispersion in prices." The temperature analogy: "If the temperature at one moment is 15 degrees but at a later time is 18 degrees, then at some intermediate time, even if only very briefly, the temperature must have also been 16 and 17 degrees."
- Jump process: "the price of a contract remains constant for a period of time, then instantaneously jumps to a new price, where it again remains constant for some period of time. ... A jump process is a combination of fixed prices and instantaneous jumps." Canonical example: how central banks set interest rates. The Fed sets the discount rate and it stays there until fixed at a new rate.

What the model assumes: a diffusion process, with trading 24 hours a day, seven days a week, without interruption, and no gaps. "If a contract trades at 46.05, and at some later time trades at 46.08, then at some intermediate time it must have also traded, even if only briefly, at 46.06 and 46.07. If one were to draw a graph of price changes under a diffusion process, one would never lift the pencil from the paper."

The violation: exchanges are not open 24 hours, so a contract closes at one price and opens the next day at a different one. Intraday, major news hits almost instantaneously and gaps prices up or down.

**Figure 18-4** (book p396). Trader thinks implied volatility is much too high and sells the 100 straddle with the future at 100; the market immediately gaps to 105. Implied Volatility = 20%; Interest Rate = 6%.

| | 9 months, futures at 100 | 9 months, futures at 105 | 1 day, futures at 100 | 1 day, futures at 105 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 call price | 6.59 | 9.41 | .42 | 5.00 |
| 100 put price | 6.59 | 4.63 | .42 | 0 |
| 100 straddle price | 13.18 | 14.04 | .84 | 5.00 |

- Nine months to expiration: the straddle rose about **7%** (14.04 / 13.18 = 1.07). "The gap was painful with nine months to expiration."
- One day to expiration: the straddle rose **495%** (5.00 / .84 = 5.95). "...but it was devastating with one day to expiration."
- Gamma of the 100 call and put: **2.2 with nine months to expiration; 38.1 with one day to expiration.**
- Mechanism: with one day left, the sold 100 calls act like short futures. After the gap the trader is naked short deeply in-the-money calls, each with a delta of 100, in a market that just leapt upward, having started approximately delta neutral. "A gap is an instantaneous move; there is no opportunity to adjust. The very high gamma, combined with an inability to make any adjustment, is what makes the gap so devastating."
- Footnote 8: the example assumes no change in implied volatility after the gap. "Admittedly, this is unlikely to be the case."
- With nine months left the gap "is unlikely to be the end of the world," since the market could easily fall back to 100, and it "is probably not disastrous." With one day left, "the trader is now in a situation where he might very well be ruined."

Why this is structural: "Options have the unique characteristic of automatically, and continuously, rehedging themselves by changing their deltas as the price of the underlying contract changes. It is this characteristic which buyers of options are paying for." A trader exploiting a mispriced option establishes a delta-neutral hedge and then performs that rehedging manually over the life of the option. When the market gaps, the assumption is violated and "the values generated by the model are rendered invalid." The same failure hits any application that replicates option characteristics through continuous rehedging: "The proponents of portfolio insurance suffered their greatest setbacks on October 19 and 20, 1987, when the market made several large gap moves. Because of the gaps, the portfolio insurers were unable to make continuous delta adjustments to their positions. As a consequence, they found that the cost of protection offered by portfolio insurance was much greater than they had ever expected."

Which options are mispriced, and which way: "Since a gap in the market will have its greatest effect on a high gamma option, and since at-the-money options close to expiration have the highest gamma, it is these options which are likely to be mispriced by a traditional theoretical pricing model with its continuous diffusion process. The closer one gets to expiration, the more suspect model-generated values become."

**Bias rule, verbatim (book p398):** "As a result of the gaps which occur in the real world, both a trader's experience and empirical evidence seem to indicate that a traditional model, with its built-in diffusion assumption, **tends to undervalue at-the-money options as expiration approaches**."

**Risk rule, verbatim:** "From a risk standpoint, this means that it can be very dangerous to sell a large number of at-the-money options close to expiration, since any gap in the underlying market can have devastating results. New traders, in particular, are advised to avoid such positions. No risk manager will appreciate even experienced traders being short large numbers of at-the-money options as expiration approaches."

What the trader does: pay less and less attention to model-generated values as expiration approaches. Floor traders carry theoretical-value sheets to make markets consistent with the model, but as expiration approaches they discard the sheets, and with one or two days left most traders simply decide from experience and intuition. "While this is perhaps unscientific, it sometimes makes better sense than trading from model-generated values when the model is known to be incorrect." The long side of this same bias (buying cheap at-the-money straddles into expiration) is the *Expiration Straddles* subsection, routed to the shared Natenberg reference document.

### 5. Volatility is independent of the price of the underlying contract

What the model assumes: the volatility input defines a one-standard-deviation price change at any time during the life of the option, regardless of whether the underlying happens to be rising or falling. Contract at 100 with 20% assumed: "If at some later time during the life of the option the contract should move up to 150 or down to 50, 20% is still assumed to be the operative volatility."

The violation, as a directional taxonomy to memorize:

| Market family | More volatile when | Natenberg's line |
|---|---|---|
| Stock index and bond markets | **Falling** | "If one were to ask a stock index or bond trader whether his market were more volatile when rising or falling, he would probably say that it was more volatile when falling." |
| Agricultural and precious metal markets | **Rising** | "Those markets tend to be more volatile when rising." |

General statement: "the volatility of a market is not independent of the price of the underlying contract. On the contrary, the volatility over time seems to be dependent on the direction of movement in the underlying contract."

Bias direction: the model prices upside and downside movement with one symmetric volatility, so it misprices whichever direction your market actually accelerates into. In a stock index or bond market the model is too cheap on the downside; in ags and precious metals it is too cheap on the upside.

What the trader does: name your market family before you trust a single volatility number across all strikes and both directions. The named alternative is the constant-elasticity of variance model, and Natenberg rejects it in practice (see below); the practical remedy is the volatility skew.

### 6. Percent price changes are normally distributed, prices lognormal at expiration

The test Natenberg runs: "Does the real world look like a lognormal distribution? One way to answer the question is to ask how percent price changes over small periods of time are distributed. If this distribution is normal, then the prices at expiration are likely to be lognormally distributed."

Method: build a frequency distribution of daily percent price changes to the nearest quarter percent over five years (1989 to 1993), compute the mean and standard deviation of all the daily changes, and overlay a theoretically exact normal distribution built from those two numbers. If the distribution were exactly normal, the tops of the bars would coincide exactly with the normal curve.

The three observed deviations:

1. **More small price changes** than a true normal predicts. The bars representing small changes rise above the curve.
2. **More large price changes** (outliers) than a true normal predicts. Several large changes rise above the extreme tails of the normal.
3. **Fewer intermediate moves** than expected. In the midsections, between the peak and the extreme tails, there are fewer occurrences than one would expect.

Generalization (book p402): "price change distributions for almost all underlying markets exhibit characteristics which are very similar to our S&P 500 distribution. There are usually more days with small moves, more days with large moves, and fewer days with intermediate moves than are predicted by a true normal distribution." Confirmed on German Bonds and on soybeans over the same five years.

Bias direction: the model assigns too little probability to the large moves that actually occur, so it undervalues the options that pay off on those moves, which is why "the marketplace appears to believe there is a better chance for a large price move in the real world than is predicted by the Black-Scholes model" and inflates the prices of options that are far out-of-the-money or deeply in-the-money.

What the trader does: stop trying to price the tails from the model and read what the marketplace has already priced into them. That is the volatility skew, and it is the sibling skill: see `natenberg-volatility-skew` for the skew (and for skewness and kurtosis, the distributional evidence behind the inflated wings).

## When to reach for a different model

Natenberg names four alternatives and rejects three of them for practical use.

| Model | The assumption it repairs | Natenberg's verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Stochastic volatility** (volatility itself is random, prediction impossible) | 3, volatility constant | "might, under some conditions, be more suitable than a traditional pricing model. At the same time, such models add another dimension of complexity to a trader's life, and for this reason are not widely used." Footnote 4: Hull and White 1987; Scott 1987; Wiggins 1987. |
| **Jump diffusion** (a Black-Scholes variation; most of the time smooth and continuous, then a gap sends the price to a new level from which diffusion resumes until the next gap) | 4, trading continuous | "if used correctly ... does give values which are probably more accurate than traditional Black-Scholes values." But it is "considerably more complex mathematically," and in addition to the five customary inputs it requires two new ones: the average size of a jump in the underlying market, and the frequency with which such jumps are likely to occur. "Unless the user can accurately estimate these new inputs, the values generated by a jump-diffusion model may be no better, and might be worse, than those generated by a traditional model." Footnote 7: Merton 1976; Beckers 1981. |
| **Constant elasticity of variance (CEV)** ("based on an assumed relationship between volatility and the price level of the underlying contract. This relationship determines the probability of price moves of various magnitudes at each moment in time. Price changes are still random under a CEV assumption, but the randomness varies with the price of the underlying contract.") | 5, volatility independent of price | "Like the jump-diffusion model, the CEV model is mathematically complex, and therefore difficult for most traders to compute. And like the jump-diffusion model it requires additional input in the form of a mathematical relationship between the volatility and price movement in the underlying contract. Given these difficulties, the CEV model has not found wide acceptance among option traders." Footnote 8: Cox and Ross 1976; Beckers 1980; Schroder 1989. |
| **Special interest-rate models** | 3, for bonds and other rate instruments, where price moves inexorably toward par | Not optional. "a traditional Black-Scholes type model is obviously inadequate for the evaluation of such products." Footnote 5: Ho and Lee 1986; Heath, Jarrow and Morton 1992. |

The general rule on switching, verbatim (book p405):

> "Initially, one might simply look for a better theoretical pricing model. If such a model exists, then it will certainly be worth replacing the old model with the new one. But 'better' is a relative term. A model might be better in the sense that it gives slightly more accurate theoretical values. But if the model is extremely complex and difficult to use, or if it requires additional inputs of which a trader cannot always be certain, then the model may merely substitute one set of problems for another. Given the fact that most traders are not theoreticians, a more realistic solution might be to use a less complex model and somehow fine-tune it so that it is consistent with the realities of the marketplace."

And on jump diffusion specifically: "Most traders take the view that whatever weaknesses are encountered in a traditional model can be best offset through intelligent decision making based on actual trading experience, rather than through the use of a more complex jump-diffusion model."

Decide by: can you estimate the extra inputs the new model demands (jump size and jump frequency, or the volatility-to-price relationship)? If not, keep the traditional model and fine-tune it with the skew.

## Failure modes

- Auditing the *inputs* (volatility, rate) and calling it done. Assumption error is a separate error class from input error; that is why this chapter exists.
- Treating "assumption is violated" as "model is useless." Natenberg's stance is the opposite: "most traders have found that pricing models, while clearly not perfect, are an invaluable tool for making decisions in the option market ... they have proven to be far better than any other method of evaluating options."
- Adopting a jump-diffusion or CEV model without being able to estimate its extra inputs. The more complex model can be worse.
- Assuming interest-rate risk is negligible on a LEAP because it is negligible on a 3-month option. Figure 18-1 shows 2-year values moving materially on 2-point rate changes.
- Selling a large number of at-the-money options into expiration because theta looks good.
- Ignoring margin capacity when sizing. The model assumes you can always hold to expiration; a margin call converts a survivable position into a realized loss.
- Forgetting that transaction costs accrue per adjustment, so a high-gamma delta-neutral program's cost scales with gamma.
- Trusting delta-neutral conversions and reversals in a stock market with short-sale restrictions, where puts are structurally inflated relative to calls.
- Believing the model's claim that the order in which volatility occurs does not matter.

## Working checklist

```
[ ] Name the model in use (Black-Scholes variant, Cox-Ross-Rubenstein, Whaley) and the market family.
[ ] 1a: any price limits, short-sale restrictions, or live tender offers on this underlying? If stock, are puts inflated vs calls?
[ ] 1c: what is my borrow/lend spread, and how much margin could this position demand before expiration? Do I have it?
[ ] 1d: count the expected adjustments over the life, price them, and subtract. High gamma means cost is a first-order term.
[ ] 2: is this option under nine months? If yes, rate risk is small. If LEAP or stock-option time spread, re-price across a rate band.
[ ] 2: in a high-rate environment, is a long-dated in-the-money American put now an early-exercise candidate (past parity, per Figure 18-1)?
[ ] 3: is volatility rising or falling? Rising means the model undervalues at-the-money options; falling means it overvalues them.
[ ] 3: is this an interest-rate instrument? If yes, a traditional model is inadequate; use a rate model.
[ ] 4: does this market gap (overnight, on news)? How many days to expiration? Near expiration the model undervalues at-the-money options.
[ ] 4: am I short a large number of at-the-money options close to expiration? If yes, cut it.
[ ] 4: with one or two days left, set the sheets aside; the deltas are as unreliable as the values.
[ ] 5: which way does this market accelerate (index and bonds when falling, ags and metals when rising)? One symmetric volatility misprices that direction.
[ ] 6: expect more small moves, more large moves, fewer intermediate moves than normal. Read the wings off the market, not off the model.
[ ] Switch models only if I can estimate the new model's extra inputs; otherwise fine-tune with the skew.
[ ] State the verdict: trade off model values, haircut them by a named amount, or do not trade off them at all.
```

## A final thought (the closing rule)

> "Because the use of a theoretical pricing model requires a trader to make so many different decisions, both with respect to the inputs into the model and the degree to which the assumptions on which the model is based are likely to be accurate, the new option trader may feel that making the right decisions is simply a matter of luck. While luck undoubtedly plays a role in the short run, in the long run those traders who are willing to put in the effort required to understand how models work always seem to come out ahead. Experienced traders know that using a model, with all its problems, is still the best way to evaluate options and manage risk.
>
> This text, like many others on options, may have left the reader with the impression that option evaluation and trading can be reduced to a series of arithmetic calculations. The science of option evaluation is an important part of any trader's education, but mathematical models are only a tool to help the trader make decisions. Successful option trading is at least as much an art as a science, and a trader must know where science leaves off, and other intangible assets, whether intuition or market feel or experience, begin. This brings us to one final point, and perhaps the most important principle of option trading: **there is no substitute for common sense**. A trader who slavishly uses a model to make every trading decision is heading for disaster. **Only a trader who fully understands what a model can and cannot do will be able to make the model his servant rather than his master**."

## Related

- [[natenberg-volatility-skew]] the practical remedy for all six assumption failures at once: infer from the marketplace's implied volatilities what the model is getting wrong, and feed the skew back in as a sixth input. Also owns skewness and kurtosis.
- [[natenberg-theoretical-edge]] the other half of model accuracy: validating the inputs and turning value versus price into a buy, sell, or no-trade call. Run both; this skill audits assumptions, that one audits inputs.
- [[natenberg-volatility-forecast]] where the volatility input comes from, and why a historical volatility graph is never a straight line, which is what breaks assumption 3.
- [[natenberg-greeks-risk-profile]] gamma and theta computation, which this audit consumes but does not teach. Gamma 2.2 versus 38.1 is why the gap is survivable at nine months and ruinous at one day.
- Existing non-Natenberg neighbours to link, not duplicate: `options-payoff` (straddle and butterfly payoff geometry), `risk-metrics-calculation` (greeks and VaR computation), `quantitative-research` (distribution statistics on a return series), `model-thinking` (generic map-versus-territory reasoning; this skill is the option-specific instance).
- Boundary: `katz-optimization-without-curvefitting` guards a trading system's parameters against curve-fitting; this audits a pricing model's structural assumptions, which is a different object.
